title: India's AI and Data Centre Ambitions Face a Power Infrastructure Reckoning
excerpt: With nearly $300 billion committed and capacity quadrupling in six years, India's data centre build-out confronts grid instability, copper shortages, and the absence of environmental regulation.
body:
• India's data centre IT capacity has quadrupled to 1.7 GW in six years, with domestic and foreign firms committing nearly $300 billion — 95% targeting hyperscale AI campuses.
  • Data centre electricity demand is projected to grow eightfold to 91 TWh by 2035, with individual clusters capable of drawing 2 GW continuously — enough to destabilise state grids.
  • The Central Electricity Authority has asked states to incorporate data centre demand into resource adequacy planning amid grid stability concerns.
  • Beyond power, the build-out faces copper shortages (an estimated 200,000 tonnes needed), water demands, and no standalone environmental regulatory framework.

As Elon Musk recently noted on The Economist's podcast, China now produces more electricity than India, the European Union, and the United States combined — a stark reminder that artificial intelligence ambitions ultimately depend on power infrastructure. For India, which processes just 5% of the world's data despite generating 20% of global data traffic, that observation lands with particular force.

Domestic conglomerates led by Adani and Reliance have committed $210 billion to data centre expansion, while Google, Amazon, and Microsoft have pledged an additional $84 billion. The Budget 2026 added a 21-year tax holiday through 2047 for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centre infrastructure — a move IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said could attract $200 billion in investment.

A Market That Quadrupled in Six Years

According to BloombergNEF, India's live IT capacity has quadrupled to 1.7 GW, making it the largest data centre market in Asia-Pacific outside China. Maharashtra accounts for 55% of total capacity, with the next wave spreading to Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh.

https://x.com/WealthEnrich/status/2092207978539827636

The pipeline is substantial: 1.3 GW is under construction and another 3.2 GW has secured land, power, and permits. NITI Aayog projects data centre IT load could reach 16 GW by 2030, while Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has set a target of 10 GW. Deloitte estimates capacity will rise from approximately 1.5 GW to 8–10 GW by 2030, with AI workloads alone requiring an additional 40–45 TWh of electricity that year.

The Grid Under Pressure

The International Energy Agency estimates India's electricity demand is rising 6.4% annually through 2030, adding more than 570 TWh over five years. Layered on that baseline, BloombergNEF projects data centre electricity consumption will grow eightfold — from 11 TWh in 2025 to 91 TWh by 2035.

The Central Electricity Authority has gone back to the drawing board. Officials are concerned that concentrated data centre hubs in Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Telangana could destabilise the national grid. Each cluster could draw approximately 2 GW continuously — what grid planners describe as a potential "grid event" for any state. The CEA is now asking states to incorporate data centre demand into resource adequacy plans.

"If we get that sequencing right, pairing data centre growth with renewables plus storage from day one, AI-driven demand can actually accelerate India's clean energy buildout rather than compete with it."

— Srivatsan Iyer, CEO, Hero Future Energies

Beyond Power: Copper, Water, and Missing Regulations

The Indian Primary Copper Producers Association estimates data centre expansion will require approximately 200,000 tonnes of copper — roughly 20 metric tonnes per megawatt of capacity. "India's AI ambition is not just a technology or power story; it is increasingly a materials and infrastructure story, with copper at its core," the association said.

Water and cooling infrastructure add further pressure, and India currently has no standalone environmental regulatory regime for AI data centres.

"AI can create substantial economic and social value, but that value should not be assessed separately from the infrastructure required to deliver it."

— Alona Geckler, Acronis

What It Means for the Diaspora

Indian-American executives at Google, Microsoft, and Amazon are directly shaping the investment decisions behind India's data centre expansion. NRI tech professionals and investors with exposure to cloud and AI companies face a dual calculus: the commercial opportunity of a market where 95% of investment targets hyperscale AI campuses, weighed against infrastructure risks that could delay returns. India's ability to store and process its own data — rather than routing 95% through foreign servers — carries broader implications for digital sovereignty.

Looking Ahead

The sequencing challenge — ensuring generation, storage, and transmission capacity are planned before demand arrives — will define whether India meets its 2030 targets. The CEA's push for state-level resource adequacy planning is a first step, but the absence of environmental regulations and the scale of materials demand suggest the infrastructure reckoning is only beginning.
